First of all, I wish to thank Sabine von Mering for introducing me to this

This work is still at a strategic and conceptual stage.
We have not yet implemented a full operational workflow.
However, we hope that this approach can help address a challenge shared by many
collection-holding institutions: the absence of unique, persistent
identifiers for people in collection management systems.
I won't spend much time making a general case for persistent identifiers.
The scientific arguments are already well-established.
People are essential for linking biodiversity data.
This has been said, no specimen exists without an agent.
It is therefore sensible to focus on identifying and linking these agents through
persistent identifiers.
In this ecosystem, Wikidata can serve as an important broker.
It enables us to connect institutional databases with other
collection-related information.
To understand the scale of the challenge, we first look at the current
representation of people in Wikidata.
Wikidata contains more than 13 million items classified as
humans.
Of course, only a small proportion of these people are directly relevant to natural
history collections. As we can see in this example, Alexander von
Humboldt is, of course, one of them.
When we filter for people connected to collection-related properties, for
example, through the property collection item set
P11146, we find approximately 30,000 individuals.
Many collections hold, for example, specimens collected by Alexander von Humboldt,
like the museums in Berlin or in Paris, and of course, many, many more.
We have a look at other relevant identifier systems such as Sobodat.
We find roughly 15,000 distinct persons.
Again, Humboldt, he also has a Sobodat ID.
Looking at the splendid database from Senckenberg, the
database Entomologists of the World, we therefore find
13,500 distinct persons referenced in Wikidata.
For the Museum für Naturkunde in Berlin, we can also consider the Wiki project
MfN Berlin Names, led by Sabine von Mering.
This project focuses on people with a documented connection to MfN.
The project currently lists approximately 1,100 people, among others,

These examples represent the result of a substantial and ongoing

There are certainly many additional databases, identifiers, and sources that could
be included. Those three are, however, probably the most relevant
for demonstrating the relation of a person to a collection object.
More than 34,000 distinct persons is already
substantial. But is this a representative number for more
than 200 years of natural history research and specimen collecting?
Perspective. I ask the more practical questions.
How many people might we expect to find in a collection such as the
collection of the MfN?
MfN holds approximately 30 million collection objects from around the world,
collected from the 18th century onwards.
For this project, we brought together every available list containing person
names that we could identify.
The raw input consisted of around 30 tables from different
sub-collections containing approximately 800,000 name strings.
These were not 800,000 people. They included spelling variants, abbreviations,
duplicated records, and so on.
Our processing workflow therefore aimed to reduce this
noise.
By deduplication, we reduced approximately 800,000 name occurrences
to around 200,000 distinct name strings.
These strings could then be grouped into roughly 13,000
clusters. However, a cluster does not always represent a
single person. Some clusters may contain different individual similar names.
Conversely, some individuals may still appear in more than one cluster.
Therefore, this is just a rough estimate.
But based on the available data, we consider it reasonable to expect
approximately 15,000 distinct people associated with
the MfN collections.
This brings us to the central problem, the identification gap in the collection
management system. Only around 1.6% of the people
represented in our central CMS are currently linked to an unambiguous
persistent identifier.
To be fair, there are additional lists in which people have already been identified
unambiguously, but these data have not yet been integrated into the central
CMS. If we include these distributed lists, we may reach approximately
10% of identified persons, which still means that
the large majority of historical and contemporary agents remain
represented only as disconnected text strings.
So how can we bridge this gap?
One option would be to add identifiers manually, one person at a time.
This is certainly possible, but with approximately 15,000 people, it is
unlikely to be completed in the near future.
The next question is obvious: Can we automate the process?
The honest answer is partly, but full automation would probably
not be a good idea. The final act of disambiguation often requires context
that is not explicitly present in our data.
This is where collection curators and domain experts remain indispensable.
Automation cannot reliably make this final decision.
The central idea is therefore to combine the large community effort
represented in Wikidata with an institutional strategy for prioritization.
There are several possible prioritization strategies.
I would like to highlight two. Option one
is to focus first on the names that occur most frequently in the collections.
This approach maximizes impact in terms of collection objects.
In our data, approximately 1,500 agents are associated
with up to 90% of collection objects.
The exact figures may change as further data sets are incorporated, but the
general pattern remains stable. A comparatively small number of people
contributed a very large number of specimens.
Identifying these people first would connect a large proportion of collection
objects to a persistent identifier relatively quickly.
Another option could be to focus on the more complex
clusters, those containing many ambiguous strings, spelling variants, or
potentially different people.
This approach may affect fewer records initially, however, it addresses the core
problem of fragmentation and improves the quality of the underlying authority data.
Neither strategy is correct. The choice depends on institutional
priorities, available expertise, and whether the immediate objective is
broad coverage or improved data quality.
Our immediate next step is the creation of a web-based
names directory. This directory will provide a structured mapping
between a name cluster, the name strings contained in that cluster,
the presence of name in various sub-collections, and a list of
potential Wikidata QIDs. This is where the
community effort represented in Wikidata becomes
especially valuable.
By comparing name strings from our collections with Wikidata labels and
aliases, we can generate more candidate matches.
That is because we can restrict the search to people who already have known
relationships to natural history collections.
Basically, the approach is the same as using a reconciliation service, but we
are using just a subset of data to reconcile against.
That restriction does not eliminate ambiguity, but it
substantially increases the probability that a matching name refers to the correct
person. In this case, we find likely candidates for A.
White.
Chris and Jacob White do not show up yet on the list of candidates.
A collection database manager will skip these strings and
might want to let the community know that those names are not associated to
collection-related properties in Wikidata.
With the ongoing community effort, it is likely that they will show up
eventually in the list of candidates during one of the next iterations.
This directory is not intended to replace expert judgment.
Its purpose is to make expert work more efficient by providing curators with
a pre-structured, evidence-based list of possible identifiers.
To conclude, bridging the gap between name strings and
persistent identifiers requires more than technical matching.
It requires institutional commitment.
It requires clear priorities and the continued involvement of
collection experts. Wikidata and related community resources
provide a valuable foundation. Automated methods can help us
organize and prioritize the data.
This will help to reduce the complexity of the task, but reliable
identification remains a collaborative process between data infrastructure
and human expertise.
The challenge continues to be to provide experts with the right workflows.
Only then we can gradually move from disconnected name strings towards a
linked data ecosystem.
